Complete Empirical Research Plan  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  

Method:  Regression-Discontinuity Design (RDD) – with a sharp discontinuity at the FICO score of 620 and (for a sub-sample of full-documentation loans) at 600.  

Why RDD fits the question  
• The 620 rule of thumb created a mechanical, discontinuous jump in secondary-market demand for loans: loans with FICO ≥ 620 were far easier and cheaper to place into non-agency MBS pools than loans with FICO < 620, even when the underlying risk was otherwise similar.  
• Originators could not change a borrower’s exact FICO on the application date, and borrowers had little ability to manipulate it precisely, so the score is as-good-as-random in a narrow window around the cutoff.  
• This gives quasi-experimental variation in the “ease of securitization.” We can therefore compare loan performance for borrowers just above vs. just below the cutoff while holding constant the hard information embodied in FICO itself.  
• To probe the role of unverifiable information, we will estimate heterogeneous discontinuity effects by documentation type (full vs. limited/no-doc) and by loan channel (broker vs. retail, if observable).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  

Running variable: borrower’s FICO score at origination (integer 300-850).  

Main cutoff: 620 (secondary cutoff 600 for full-doc loans).  

Treatment variable (T):  AboveCutoff = 1{FICO ≥ 620}.  
Interpretation : loans just above 620 faced a large positive shock to the probability of being sold/securitized; thus originators had a lower marginal benefit from costly screening.  

Control group: loans with FICO just below 620 (e.g., 580-619 depending on chosen bandwidth).  

Timing: the “event” (ease-of-sale shock) is contemporaneous with loan origination; therefore the design is cross-sectional around the cutoff. Outcomes (e.g., 90-day delinquency, foreclosure) are measured over horizons such as 12, 24, and 36 months after origination.  

Heterogeneity/two-way RDD: we will estimate separate discontinuities for  
a) limited/no-documentation loans (where soft information matters most) and  
b) full-documentation loans (where hard, verifiable information dominates).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  

A1.  No precise manipulation of the running variable: borrowers/lenders cannot perfectly “bunch” just above 620.  
• Plausibility: FICO is based on historical credit data; manipulating it by a few points in the short window before application is difficult.  

A2.  Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff absent treatment.  
• Plausibility: there is no regulation, subsidy, or pricing rule that also changes discretely at 620 other than securitization demand. GSE conforming limits, HOEPA triggers, etc. are unrelated to 620.  

A3.  Local SUTVA: treatment of one loan does not spill over to a neighbor’s loan within the narrow FICO window.  
• Plausibility: borrower-level outcomes are independent.  

A4.  Same functional relationship in a narrow window: within the chosen bandwidth, unobserved determinants of default vary smoothly with FICO.  
• Plausibility: credit risk is monotone and smooth in FICO by construction.  

A5.  For heterogeneity analysis, documentation status itself does not jump at the cutoff (checked empirically).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATION  

Threat 1: Manipulation or bunching of FICO scores at 620.  
• Test the density of FICO using McCrary (2008). Use “donut” RDD excluding ±1–2 FICO points if bunching exists.  

Threat 2: Sample-selection bias because the main data set only contains securitized loans.  
• Use the servicer data on prime/agency loans to estimate first-stage discontinuities in securitization probability; re-weight the sample (Lee 2009) or implement a fuzzy-RDD IV where securitization status is instrumented by AboveCutoff.  
• Show that key covariates and loan terms remain smooth at the cutoff even in the securitized-only sample.  

Threat 3: Other contractual terms (rate, pre-payment penalty, LTV) could also change at 620 and mechanically affect default.  
• Include those terms as controls in the RDD; document that they do not jump, or if they do, treat them as mediators and decompose effects.  
• Placebo tests on ex-ante hard-information outcomes (e.g., appraisal value errors) that should not respond to screening effort.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R CODE OUTLINE  

```r
# ---- 0. Packages ----
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast OLS with fixed effects
library(rdrobust)    # RDD estimators
library(rddensity)   # McCrary test
library(ggplot2)

# ---- 1. Data Loading ----
dt <- fread("loanperformance_subprime_2001_2006.csv")

# ---- 2. Sample Restrictions ----
dt <- dt[
  purpose == "purchase" &
  occ_status == "owner" &
  property_type %in% c("SF","Townhouse","Condo") &
  !is.na(fico) & fico >= 560 & fico <= 680  # keep symmetric window first
]

# ---- 3. Variable Construction ----
dt[, above620  := as.integer(fico >= 620)]
dt[, above600  := as.integer(fico >= 600)]
dt[, delin90_24 := as.integer(max90dpd_first24mths >= 1)]  # example
dt[, lowdoc    := documentation %in% c("Limited","NoDoc")]

# Controls
dt[, ltv_cat := cut(ltv, breaks=c(0,80,90,100,500), labels=FALSE)]
dt[, yq := paste0(year(orig_date), "Q", quarter(orig_date))]

# ---- 4. Graphical Check ----
ggplot(dt, aes(x=fico, y=delin90_24)) +
  geom_smooth(method="loess", span=.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept=620, lty=2)

# ---- 5. McCrary Density Test ----
rddensity(dt$fico, c = 620)

# ---- 6. Main Sharp RDD (pooled) ----
rd_out <- rdrobust(y = dt$delin90_24, x = dt$fico, c = 620,
                   covs = dt[, .(ltv, rate = int_rate, lowdoc)],
                   kernel = "triangular")
summary(rd_out)

# ---- 7. Heterogeneity: Limited/No-Doc vs Full ----
for(doc in c(0,1)){
  sub <- dt[lowdoc == doc]
  cat("Documentation =", doc,"\n")
  print( rdrobust(sub$delin90_24, sub$fico, c = 620) )
}

# ---- 8. Donut RDD Robustness ----
donut <- dt[fico <= 618 | fico >= 622]
rd_donut <- rdrobust(donut$delin90_24, donut$fico, c=620)
summary(rd_donut)

# ---- 9. Placebo Cutoffs ----
placebos <- c(590, 605, 635, 650)
placebo_results <- lapply(placebos, function(cut)
  rdrobust(dt$delin90_24, dt$fico, c = cut)$coef[1])
placebo_results
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. EXPECTED RESULTS  

Prediction:  Because securitization is easier just above 620, originators devote less costly effort to gather and verify soft information, so the ex-post default rate should be higher (not lower) for loans barely above the cutoff relative to barely below.  

Magnitude: Prior studies of subprime discontinuities suggest a 2–4 percentage-point increase in 24-month 90-day-plus delinquency for above-cutoff loans, on a base of roughly 15 %. The effect should be concentrated in limited/no-doc loans and largely absent in full-doc loans.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (RDD)  

C1: Continuity of running-variable density at cutoff ………………… 1  
C2: Continuity of baseline covariates at cutoff …………………………… 1  
C3: No other policy or pricing jump at cutoff …………………………… 0.5 (interest rate menu could jump slightly)  
C4: Correct functional form / bandwidth choice ……………………… 1  
C5: Robustness to placebo cutoffs & donut test ……………………… 1  

Overall: 4.5 / 5 – strong but must guard against sample-selection and contractual-term confounds.
